title: {{NAME}} and the Temporal Response Squad
moral: Preparation means that when the extraordinary happens, you are ready for it.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a dark steel-blue hero suit with amber temporal markings, armoured boots, and amber gauntlets — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} had designed the Temporal Response Squad's toolkit for exactly one purpose: handle prehistoric animal displacement events safely, swiftly, and without harm to any party.

The toolkit included: WARD (a containment robot with non-harmful barrier technology), a tranquiliser array that had never needed to be used, a communication module for animal signalling, and forty-seven protocols built from the squad's previous twelve deployments.

Deployment thirteen: a Gallimimus flock of nine, a Brachiosaurus, and a Pachycephalosaurus, all arriving simultaneously in a residential park.

"Thirteen at once," said {{NAME}}. "That's a new record."

No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
Protocol priority: the Gallimimus first, as fast-moving panicked animals were the highest public safety risk.

WARD deployed three soft barriers in a funnel configuration. The Gallimimus followed the funnel because Gallimimus followed open corridors. It was in the data from deployments three and seven.

{{NAME}} managed the Brachiosaurus with the communication module: three tones that meant slow down and look here. It stopped examining the climbing frame and turned toward him.

The Pachycephalosaurus was still in the path. Still displeased.

"One thing at a time," {{NAME}} said.

Dynamic organised scene, WARD's barriers guiding the Gallimimus flock, {{NAME}} using the communication module on the Brachiosaurus, the park around them being managed with practiced calm. No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
The Pachycephalosaurus, he discovered from the data, responded to one specific signal: the smell of particular vegetation, combined with an open sight line.

He sent WARD to create the sight line (it was WARD's third function, opening corridors in confined spaces).

He provided the vegetation from the park's botanical area.

The Pachycephalosaurus moved toward the open corridor and followed the scent.

Ninety-two minutes from arrival to all eleven animals contained and calm.

Previous record for this size event: four hours.

"Forty-seven protocols," he said to WARD. "Forty-eight now."

All eleven animals now calm in their designated areas, {{NAME}} and WARD surveying the completed operation, the park quiet, everything managed. No text, no words, no letters anywhere in the image.

pages.content:
The squad director reviewed the report the next morning.

"Ninety-two minutes for eleven animals. This is the best response we've ever logged."

"WARD handled the Gallimimus and the corridor," said {{NAME}}. "The protocols handled the rest."

"You wrote the protocols."

"After deployments one through twelve," said {{NAME}}. "The deployments taught me."

The director looked at him. "How old are you?"

"Eleven," said {{NAME}}.

Long pause. "Right."

pages.content:
He walked home through the park where the deployment had been.

The grass was slightly compressed in the Gallimimus area. The climbing frame had a small mark from the Brachiosaurus.

Otherwise: completely normal.

Invisible heroism. The best kind.

In bed that night, he added deployment thirteen to his notebook and wrote: forty-eight protocols now. Next time, forty-nine.

He fell asleep before he could write what the forty-ninth would be.

His hand was still on the page when the lamp clicked off automatically.
